newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH LEFT VICTORY MAY HERALD SHIFT IN EUROPE.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH LEFT VICTORY MAY HERALD SHIFT IN EUROPE.

text.p: France's Socialist Party swept to power in a parliamentary election on Sunday promising a new direction in European policies and heralding a shift in the way Europe puts together its plans for a single currency in 1999.

Analysts said the left's upset victory over the ruling centre-right coalition, combined with political crisis in Germany over budget problems, pointed to a profound change under way in preparations for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"It looks as if the conservative era is coming to an end," Eckhard Schulte, IBJ economist in Frankfurt, said.
"There is a demand for a change in policy on the economy and on Europe," UBS economist Eric Muller said.
"This is a great success for France and for Europe," left-wing German opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine said.
"With it are linked the people's hopes for a reduction in unemployment and for more social justice," Lafontaine, chairman of the Social Democrats, said in a congratulatory message.

Economists said French voters had rejected the policies of austerity meant to comply with a German-led vision of Europe where only those with a solid track record on economic policies would be allowed into a hard-core EMU.

Everything now was pointing to a fudging of Maastricht Treaty EMU entry requirements, and wider membership of a single currency -- increasing the threat of a reaction from the German people who might eventually insist on delaying the whole thing.

"The odds are that (Socialist leader Lionel) Jospin will want to make the euro more and more of a marshmalllow. That is precisely what German citizens are most worried about," Paul Horne, economist at Smith Barney in Paris, said.

"In both countries, Germany and France, fiscal consolidation and austerity is going to be very difficult," Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt, said. "The risks for EMU have increased somewhat, but I still don't believe that the EMU process is going to be derailed."
France's combined left, confirming a lead in first-round voting, won in a landslide in the runoff vote.
Hailing the victory, Jospin described the vote as "a demand for a reorientation of European construction, which we favour".

The Socialist Party is committed to launching a single currency, but is demanding a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty, a European "economic government" and early membership for Italy, Spain and Portugal.
Jospin has also said he does not feel bound by the European Union's "stability pact", agreed last year and meant to limit budget deficits after the euro's launch.
Economists said they believed the Socialist Party, which negotiated Maastricht under late president Francois Mitterrand, were unlikely to take big risks with the EMU plans.

They were likely to try to establish their credibility initially in the eyes of financial markets and back President Jacques Chirac, who retains ultimate control of foreign policy, in the drive towards monetary union.
"I know what President Chirac's programme is, and he's still in office," European Commission President Jacques Santer told reporters.
But the change in government in France nonetheless comes at a time when the single-currency project is looking fragile.
German's government is embroiled in a row with the Bundesbank over a revaluation of gold to bolster the country's flagging public finances.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl was holding crisis talks on Sunday night to try to defuse the gold row and plug holes in the German budget without blowing apart the coalition government.
Kohl's coalition partners, the liberal Free Democrats, have said they oppose tax hikes to limit the budget deficit.
The big questions now are what will happen to the political make-up in Germany, and whether the German people can accept the new change of emphasis in France or will push for a delay.
"I think many people in Germany will now discuss the euro much more intensively than they have done so far," Schulte said.
"The majority of (French) voters decided to elect a party which favours a fudge (of Maastricht Treaty criteria) and a broad EMU. It's now fudge or delay. The ball is in the German camp," he said.
